document.title: PDD 39, U.S. Policy on Counterterrorism
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
document.note: [Secret] 12-page directive on reducing vulnerabilities, deterring and responding to terrorism, and WMD. It directs the FBI, Transportation, the DCI (aggressive intelligence collection, analysis, counterintelligence and covert action) and FEMA. It states the U.S. will induce cooperation from states harboring wanted terrorists and may return suspects by force without host government cooperation.

organizations.name: The White House

organizations.name: Department of State

organizations.name: Department of Justice

organizations.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation

organizations.name: Central Intelligence Agency

organizations.name: Federal Emergency Management Agency

places.name: United States

events.description: White House issues memorandum PDD-39 setting U.S. policy on counterterrorism: deter, defeat and respond to terrorist attacks, no concessions to terrorists, pressure on state sponsors, and return of indicted terrorists for prosecution.
PDD 39 directs lead agency designations, EST (FEST/DEST) structure, hijacking and consequence-management responsibilities, cost-bearing, and top priority for countering terrorist WMD acquisition.
President Clinton issues PDD-39 setting U.S. counterterrorism policy: deter, defeat, respond to terrorism; no concessions to terrorists; isolate state sponsors.
PDD-39 directs Attorney General to chair a Cabinet Committee reviewing vulnerability of government facilities and critical infrastructure.
PDD-39 validates lead agency responsibilities, designating State as lead for incidents abroad.

key_claims: US policy is to make no concessions to terrorists and to treat terrorism as both a national security threat and a criminal act.
The US will identify, isolate and extract a heavy price from states and groups that sponsor or support terrorists.
Return of indicted terrorists to the US for prosecution is a highest priority and a central issue in bilateral relations with harboring states.
Return of suspects by force may be effected without host government cooperation under NSD-77 procedures.
The State Department is the lead agency for terrorist incidents abroad, acting through US ambassadors as on-scene coordinators.
Terrorist acquisition of weapons of mass destruction is deemed unacceptable and the highest priority to prevent.
